introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).
incertitudes: Le corrigé présente la thèse musulmane sur le statut des livres antérieurs (tahrif) comme telle et rappelle que juifs et chrétiens tiennent leurs Écritures pour authentiques (neutralité).

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY ». Cette règle (4 questions d'UNE SEULE section) n'est pas exprimable avec `parmi` (un seul groupe) ni `ou` (sous-questions) : `regles_choix` reste vide dans tous les fichiers et la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source ; les références sont limitées à des passages et faits bien établis, les autres points sont formulés prudemment. À faire relire par un spécialiste des études religieuses avant mise en avant.

questions.enonce_markdown: Critically examine the belief in the books in Islam. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Belief in the revealed books is one of the six articles of faith (iman) in Islam, with belief in God, angels, messengers, the Last Day and divine decree. The Qur'an says that believers believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers (Surah al-Baqarah, verse 285). This answer explains the belief and examines it critically.

**1. Content of the belief.**
- God sent guidance to humanity through messengers, and He revealed books to some of them: the Tawrat (Torah) to Musa, the Zabur (Psalms) to Dawud, the Injil (Gospel) to Isa, and the Qur'an to Muhammad. The Qur'an also mentions the scrolls (suhuf) of Ibrahim.
- All the books share one message: worship of the one God and moral responsibility.
- The Qur'an is the last and final revelation; Muslims believe it confirms what was true in earlier books and acts as a standard over them.

**2. Strengths and importance.**
- It makes Muslims respect earlier prophets and the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), and so supports a sense of continuity with Judaism and Christianity.
- It protects the unity of the message: God does not contradict Himself.
- It gives the Qur'an its authority: Muslims are to follow the last, preserved guidance.
- It is one of the conditions of faith; denying a revealed book is a denial of faith.

**3. Critical points.**
- *Status of earlier books.* Muslims hold that the books as now possessed by Jews and Christians do not preserve the original revelation in full (tahrif), and that the Qur'an is preserved. Jews and Christians themselves believe that their scriptures are authentic, and historians study the long process of their formation. This is a point of difference between the traditions.
- *Practical consequence.* Most Muslims do not use the older books as a source of law, so belief in them is largely a matter of faith and respect rather than practice.
- *Differences in content.* On matters such as the nature of Jesus and the cross, the Qur'an and the Christian Gospels differ, so Muslims explain the difference through the view that the original message was altered.
- *Basis of the claim.* The belief is accepted on faith in the Qur'an's own statements, so it is not open to independent proof.

**Conclusion.** The belief is coherent within Islam: it links the faith to earlier revelations while giving the Qur'an final authority. It brings respect for other scripture-based communities, but it also contains claims about earlier books that other traditions do not accept.
